report:
**Conclusion:** Your skepticism is justified. The claim that *eating dark chocolate lowers stroke risk* is not established as a causal health benefit.

- The positive evidence is mostly **observational** and concerns *chocolate generally*, not reliably dark chocolate or a standardized cocoa-flavanol dose. A 2012 meta-analysis of five prospective cohorts found lower stroke incidence in the highest versus lowest chocolate-intake groups (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.73–0.90), but such studies cannot fully rule out healthier lifestyle, socioeconomic, dietary, or medical differences between chocolate eaters and non-eaters.  
  https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22933736/

- Findings are inconsistent. In the large Women’s Health Initiative cohort, chocolate intake was **not associated** with stroke risk (linear-trend P=0.24).  
  https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6862600/

- Randomized evidence does not demonstrate stroke prevention from chocolate. COSMOS tested a **600-mg/day cocoa-flavanol extract** (not ordinary dark chocolate) and did not significantly reduce its primary outcome of total cardiovascular events, although some secondary findings were promising. It therefore cannot establish that eating dark chocolate prevents strokes.  
  https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35294962/

- Cocoa flavanols plausibly affect blood-vessel function: EFSA concluded they can maintain normal endothelium-dependent vasodilation. But that is a short-term physiological effect, **not proof of fewer strokes**.  
  https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2012.2809

So, “may be associated with lower stroke risk” is a fair description of limited observational evidence; “dark chocolate lowers stroke risk” overstates it. Dark chocolate also varies greatly in flavanol content and can add substantial calories, sugar, and saturated fat.
